reviews.text: > Explored an alien planet > Ran out of oxygen > Crewmate Sarah picked up an alien disease > Symptoms are Lung inflammation, Cough, Fever, and Death > Sarah spread disease to everyone in the ship > Everyone died of Coronavirus I play games to escape reality, thank you very much. ========================================== However, for an actual review of the paltry amount that I have played, it is very enjoyable so far. The only annoyance so far is with how planets and oxygen function. At the moment, you have a certain amount of oxygen when you land - I had 69 for my first run. Each tile you walk across or action you take (like shooting enemies) uses one unit of oxygen. That leaves you with about 35 actions of exploration before you have to return to your ship and refuel your oxygen. There are suit upgrades you can purchase for the ground crew, but I haven't found any that actually increase the oxygen amount. Right now, it just feels like a tedious way to stretch out gameplay. Yes it's 'realistic', but it's not really that fun to have to stop exploring, run back to your ship, run back through your explored area, and then explore two or three more tiles before having to run back again. Besides that though, the game has a lot of great systems and things working for it, even if it is a bit obfuscated by the UI - which shouldn't be a new concept to most classic Roguelike players. The procedural crafting is neat, the customization at the beginning is pretty cool, and the artifacts/history system is interesting as well. It took a run or two to get comfortable with the UI and how to do certain things, but there's a lot to it. Though, I do wish there was more than one space station per area. Ability to play by keyboard alone, or by Mouse alone which is great, since I often flip between enjoying each control mode over the other.

One of the best rogue-like's ever made. I have 100's of hours into AI 1.0-1.3. Now it has been upgraded with enhanced graphics, gameplay, UI scaling, etc. to run on modern machines and displays. It's already better than AI 1.3 at Early Access release! If you play rogue-likes or similar, or if this game seems even remotely interesting to you, get it right now!

I wish I could make this review Neutral - this game seems like it has a lot of potential, but in an hour and a half of playing I saw the same four enemies repeated infinitely across every planet I visited, every map was a wide open world with nothing interesting to find, every piece of cargo existed only to be sold. There's not much depth to the mechanics - ranged weapons have infinite ammo, away team crew is extremely easy to replace, enemies don't have any special abilities and seem to be all melee (on land) or just stand still and shoot at you (in space). This would be fine in a casual roguelike but the scope of this game made me want something more complex with a lot more fiddling with my crew or loadout or ship. I'm considering re-buying it since it's only $10 and the amount of content I saw was light enough to be almost shocking (so I feel like I must have been missing something) so it does have that element of sort-of-intrigue going for it. Right now Star Traders: Frontiers does everything that this game does better than this game does, but I definitely have an interest in seeing where Approaching Infinity is at in a couple months.
Get dizzying space sickness, go to a station for the cure. The cure has been recalled and I'm told to practice social distancing. 100/100 Best game.

My time isn't close - I've played probably more than 1000 hours (from the pre-steam version...) If that alone isn't enough to tell you that there is lots to do, then not sure what else will convince you. There is a lot going on in the game. While it is relatively simple and strait-forward to play, you really need to think about what you are doing all the time because the tactical and strategic choices are abundant. Do you sell off old components for $$, or salvage for crafting parts? Is it better to have long range or less fuel use for warp drive? What about cool down time? With virtually every item in the game you need to balance needs to survive. Even walking can have deep impacts. Go one step too far (or in the wrong direction) and you might kill off your away team. And nowhere else will be so torn on what to do about bunnies. They're so cute and soft, and impassable. That one time they block your path and kill off your away team you will know the terror! "Kill the Wabbit!" Its a great roguelike in space, and will have lots for you to do for a long time. And as a bonus, this version already has many improvements over the previously available version (from another online store). Nov 2023 Update: Its still getting better. If you aren't playing, you really are missing out!
I can belive someone in the reviews compared this to caves of qud. This game sucks.

I am a wee bit biased being the one who did the graphics for this game, but the good news is I wouldn't invest all the time and effort if the game wasn't good. It combines two of my favorite genres Sci fi and Roguelikes. This game has allot of game play and the longer you play and the further you go, the more interesting things you discover. And new stuff and tweaking is done every day, the latest patch is a testament to how well IBOL is listening to your feedback. No game succeeds without a growing and active community. I'm a part of this community and I'm not leaving any time soon. Se you on the discussion boards and Have fun! Cheers! (lol, Steam wants me to say I got the game for free, Hello? o/ Dev Team member here! lol) Cheers v2.0!

While Approaching Infinity currently doesn't have the same tactical depth you might find in other traditional roguelikes, it's still fun to explore the universe and interact with its various races and creatures as you upgrade your ship and away team, promote your captain and other officers to learn new skills, and trade, mine asteroids, or attack other ships as you generally encounter weird space things. Although it's rough around the edges, AI is already very playable and IBOL17 is a very active and dedicated dev, responsive to feedback and constantly working on updates and new features, even recently quitting his day job to develop Approaching Infinity full time now that there's enough financial support. Kudos, man :) So if you're ready for a laid back space exploration roguelike, this is the game for you and it'll keep you occupied for a while, with no doubt even more content to explore down the line. I started playing Approaching Infinity recently for my weekly stream, enjoying it with chat as we learned the game and talked about its design. IBOL showed up for a bit in the first stream, too: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uzgX32bzFTM
买之前还以为是那种大地图随机生成的模式，实际买来发现他们把一张张地图称为sector每张地图都有warp可以跳转到其他地图上，一般一张地图上会有几个可以登录的星球，飞船残骸，其他势力的基地，资源，太空海盗以及一个贸易中心。贸易中心里面可以买卖物资，购买飞船配件以及维修飞船，也可以买新飞船等等。对我来说很新颖，因为没玩过科幻类肉鸽游戏。但是不是大地图的模式让人有点失望。

I loved this game when it first came out. I thought it was great. But I fired it up just now and found that the devs had replaced the old style mechanic of the game getting more difficult according to what sector you were in (sectors are basically dungeon levels or they were at one time anyway), and now have some sort of weird Bethesda-like level scaling mechanic where the difficulty can suddenly ramp up enormously even though you're in the same area you were 10 minutes ago. It's not even clear to the playerbase what it is that causes the scaling, whether it's player level or equipment or the overall capability of your ship and crew. Sorry, but this irritates me on two levels. 1. I really, really hate when devs take a good game that I bought and later tinker with it and mess it up. This happens too often. 2. As a roguelike fan, it's almost offensive to me to see level scaling like this in a roguelike. I'm grimacing as I type this, in the way you would if a cockroach scuttled across your hand or something. It's rare that I'm actually annoyed when I write a review but lord, that's annoying. Level scaling in a roguelike... gtfoh with that.

For being a roguelike, the game is shockingly easy, and weirdly simple. The current systems don't allow for much in the way of play diversity, variation, or interesting decision making. But more than anything, the game just isn't very fun. There isn't a lot to do, and what is there isn't very interesting. Some people seem to really like it, and no doubt the dev is passionate. But I'm not going to recommend this game, not without a few more years of development.

Not sure what these positive reviews are saying... there's comparisons to dungeon crawl stone soup, caves of qud, cogmind, etc. The above mentioned games are deep, can be replayed many times in many different ways, and generally have great depth. This game does not. I don't mean to be really critical but this isn't even close to any of the pillars of the genre and I have the very strong impression that a lot of these reviews are bought. There's nowhere near the depth of CoQ, DCSS, CDDA, TOME, ADOM, etc. It's really not even close at all. All of the positive reviews have the same suspicious format... I would be very wary of buying this and expecting a fully functioning roguelike experience. It's just not there. This is a very simple game with very simple progression and there's a very large lack of meaningful choices or things to learn.

已提名2024年”爱的付出奖“，为了完成任务”更新一篇已提名的游戏的测评“而更新本段内容。说实话，这个奖我一般要么提名cogmind，要么提名caves of qud，前几年都是如此；但后来我发现，即便是这俩传统RL的行业支柱也逐渐放缓了更新的步伐，而该游戏的作者却一直保持着不低的更新频率，所以今年改城提名它了。其实在当年测评完之后我就没有再玩过该游戏，也不知道它现在更新到了什么地步，但我确实敬佩这种精神。原来的测评我推荐15元左右入手，现在可能这个参考价格可以更高一些了。 ------------------- 这是一个小体量的游戏，完全的新鲜感大约能维持15个小时左右（但并不意味着15个小时后就会无聊）。是的，中文名叫逼近无限，你也确实可以深入到无限层星空中去，但无限的本质终究只是一个函数，玩家终有察觉的一天。 平时你操控飞船在星空中巡航，在星站中购买物资和接受任务，或与敌方飞船直接在星空中爆发战斗。也可以降落到星球上去探险，此时星空地图就切换成了地表地图，而你则操纵探险队，靠收集地形资料和捡垃圾发财，必要时和怪物发生战斗。 所以这游戏的玩点在于它的两套培养体系：飞船和探险队。探险队由N名队长带领，每种职业的队长都有独特的主动和被动技能（总共将近几十个吧），对飞船或探险队本身都有巨大影响。飞船的组成部件都是有等级的，随着深入星空，不断更换高级部件实质上也是对飞船的升级。此外该游戏还有外交系统，炼金系统等，就不细说了。 每片星空其实就是一张地图，里面有一个时空旋涡，进去后就能进入下一片星空的地图。所以，这个游戏的地图模板严格来说只有4张：一张是星空地图，一张是地表地图，一张是地表下的地牢地图，一张是飞船残骸地图（飞船残骸类似于星球，可着陆探索），剩下的就是根据函数随机生成。大部分任务也是根据一定规律随机生成的，比如在X星空接任务，到Y星空搜集Z资源，然后交给当地的星站；而当地星站的任务又是到下一片星空搜另外的资源，只不过敌人更强一些，报酬会多一些。 千篇一律？不尽然。事实上，我在25个小时之后依旧兴趣盎然，这是因为虽然地图不咋样，但其他内容较为丰富：我还有十几种飞船类型没解锁、超过一半的职业技能没用过，主线任务也没认真做，这些东西显然就不是根据函数随机生成的了，而且目前还是EA阶段，话不能说太满。另外，这个游戏绝对不是那种纯粹的刷刷刷游戏，很需要策略，经常是强敌环伺，需要你利用地形来出奇制胜，具体就不展开了。 购买建议：15元左右（当前史低33元）。

Repetitive enemies, no real hook with gameplay mechanics. Average game over all and doesn't stick out in any way shape or form. Worth playing if those factors don't bother you and you want a simple easy to play rougelike

Take a look at the achievement list, and it should give you some idea of what you'll be doing: The same things again and again forever, while number goes up. A lot of things are procedurally generated, but it's all surface-level. There just aren't enough systems in the game to interact and create "emergent novelty," or whatever you'd call the thing that makes games like Dwarf Fortress and Rimworld legendary.

强力推荐，非常好玩的游戏，而且看似是个小体量游戏，里面的内容真的一点都不少，刚入门的时候大概需要花10小时左右的时间来让自己有能力存活到10象限以上，并且在入门期结束后会惊讶地发现原来后面还有新内容，我估计所有新鲜的东西彻底消失大概需要旅行到35-40象限的位置，真的相当好玩了。 其实玩这个游戏很容易陷入一个误区，平时大家玩这种闯关类的肉鸽游戏一般都不会走回头路，但是这个游戏实际上是鼓励你在不同象限之间来回穿梭的，熟悉这一点之后玩起来就舒服很多，前期觉得解决不了的地图全都可以留到后面再来处理，或者是前期看到了属性好的废船但是没有材料，完全可以放个标记等后期废料能无限刷了再回来修复。 作者更新也挺勤快的，而且能看到很多留了空但是还没出的内容，未来可期。
几百小时都会有不同的内容，100象限以后会有很多奇奇怪怪的星域。目前不知道纳米星球怎么建造，难道是自己打造一个小星球？制造等级分解未知图纸，但是到100多以后图纸越来越少，不知道如何提升了，总之这个小体量的游戏非常亮眼。好评，推荐推荐！！

Incredible rougelike. There’s so much content and variety and different skills and ways to play. It’s a lot different from the traditional rougelike loop of survive till you find OP items and then win. It’s a lot more about how you explore and interact with the galaxy in an RPG sense. For instance, I was playing an ecology/scientist type character. I spent all my time running from fights, landing on planets and studying every animal and plant on them. I thought it was odd that I only got XP from killing the animals so I asked the dev if an option to peacefully study the animals as an ecologist would be possible, and the dev agreed and put it in the next update! From then on I kept “peacefully” exploring and selling ecological data and was confused as to why so many factions hated me, only to find I had been selling all my data to the most hated faction just cuz they had paid the most! Plays great on steam deck as well, it’s the perfect type of pick and and play game for it
come for no man's qud, stay for a unique and compelling roguelike experience. absolutely fantastic 10/10

Full disclosure: I wrote the soundtrack for Approaching Infinity... ... in 2013. In case you were wondering, it is currently 2025. Somehow, Bob kept at it for 12 more years. Meanwhile, I had no idea the game was in development after I sent Bob the soundtrack all those years ago. Imagine my surprise when a friend called me a couple of weeks ago telling me that the game had been released. Super happy for Bob to have finally finished his magnum opus. Even happier that it has been so well-received! It has a little bit of everything that makes hardcore roguelikes so compelling. If you're a fan of the genre, you'll be a fan of Approaching Infinity!

ChatGPT recommended me this game when I asked for things like Caves of Qud. So buddy - AI is on your side with this one! I've only played for a few hours now, but it starts feeling like Civ in "one more turn" way. I was a little put off at first the galaxy being a "line", bus as other reviewers have mentioned it's not really an issue once you get going. I also like that it awards completionism. You can "complete" planets you find in your journeys, which then rewards you with a scan that you can sell for $$ at any station, but also makes that planet "unvisitable" again so you're not spinning wheels revisiting planets you've already completed in search of the ones not done yet. But it's not as easy as just walking everywhere, as planets have geographical features that might make it impossible to map without special equipment. For example, i've landed on a water world, where most of tiles were water. Impossible to map on food - but gladly i had equiped a waterwalking upgrade for my away team, so i was able to map the planet, while also collecting special resources that are located only inside the bodies of water. I feel like i'll be spending lots of time here, possibly more than in Star Traders.
Game of the year for me.

Far more than meets the eye, I sat down to play a quick game and get everything figured out and 10 hours later went to bed muttering to myself about how tired I would be tomorrow. Lots of fun, a bunch to do and many different interesting interactions that keep you dropping down to just one more planet.

[h1]A Brief Review of Approaching Infinity[/h1] Approaching Infinity is absolutely stellar. Unfortunately, I’m spectacularly bad at it. I make catastrophically poor decisions with impressive consistency. Every run is a glorious zero-gravity dumpster fire—and I love it. [b]CAPTAIN’S LOG[/b] Our mission to explore the unknown continues... poorly. I remain deeply committed to charting my crew’s success. Unfortunately, today I attempted first contact with an alien that turned out to be sentient radiation. The crew is still glowing. After a bit of research—and some questionably ethical medical experimentation—I managed to develop a serum to counteract the radiation. The result: the crew is now bio-luminescent and speaks exclusively in palindromes. Honestly? I’m calling it a win. So far, I’ve been sued by a sentient asteroid for “reckless orbiting,” banned from a planet for starting an accidental space cult, and somehow got promoted by my crew for reasons no one fully understands. Morale is high, mostly because I’ve rerouted oxygen to the karaoke machine. Tactical mistakes are frequent—yesterday I accidentally jettisoned half the cargo, the science officer, and my pants. We press on. [b]END LOG.[/b] [b]CREW LOG, PLEASE SEND HELP![/b] To Central Command: The captain continues to describe our mission as a "glorious adventure into the stars." Following yesterday’s incident with the sentient radiation (and the now bio-luminescent crew), the captain declared it a “scientific victory” and passed out glowsticks in celebration. The science officer is missing (again). No one is sure if he was jettisoned, vaporized, or is simply hiding in one of the boxes of boxes. Oxygen continues to be rerouted to the karaoke machine. I have filed multiple complaints. Each complaint was returned with glitter and a note that read, “Sing your feelings.” Our official ship name has been registered in this sector as “Funky Town” without crew vote. Please advise. [b]END LOG.[/b] Despite overwhelming evidence that I should not be in charge of anything with thrusters, Approaching Infinity continues to deliver the most glorious cosmic chaos I’ve ever thoroughly enjoyed. [b]PROS[/b] *The Dev is the bomb—patches drop faster than my ships explode, and community feedback actually matters. *The game rewards curiosity—and occasionally punishes it with a surprise black hole or a strongly worded letter from space clowns. You never know if that shiny object is rare loot or the start of an interstellar incident. *Every run is like unwrapping a neon space piñata filled with loot, lasers, and deeply questionable life choices. Between the procedural chaos, faction drama, and loot that may or may not explode, the galaxy offers endless, spectacular ways to die—and I’m here for all of them. *You get to choose your pain level. Want chill exploration? Cool. Want a permadeath meat grinder? Also cool. The game bends, but it doesn't break. *Feels like a living game, not just a product. The community’s tight-knit, the dev listens, and bugs vanish faster than my crew gets spaced—which, frankly, is starting to feel like a core mechanic. [b]CONS[/b] *Planets will tempt you with glowing things. Glowing things are rarely friendly. That’s not loot—that's a possessed lava lamp with a bad attitude and abandonment issues. *The captain creator—complete with sliders—is my personal nemesis. This might just be a me problem, but I cannot, for the life of me, make a decent male captain. No joke—despite aiming for a grizzled male military veteran, my last two attempts somehow turned into Vulcan ladies. I wasn’t even trying for a Star Trek vibe, yet both runs ended up led by what can only be described as T’Pol’s chaotic evil twin. At this point, I’ve accepted that my crew takes orders from a vaguely confused space elf with cheekbones sharp enough to pierce the hull. [b][i]HUMBLE REQUEST:[/i][/b] Tried the demo a while back but couldn’t make a captain I liked, so I deleted the game. Glad I gave it another shot on a whim—would’ve missed out. Suggestion: add even more example captains for those of us who struggle with the customizer. *Dev pours years into a deep, intelligent game—and I use it to challenge aliens to interpretive dance battles and name my ships things like “Enterprise Rental,” “USS Hull Breach,” “The Salty Nebula” (pirate ship, obviously), “The Honking Void” (every warp emits a sad trombone), and “Space Clown Negotiator.” *Great game. Shame about the player base. (By which I mean me. Just me.)

Listen. It's a mechanically solid two-layer traditional roguelike. There's nothing innovative to write home about gameplay wise, and nothing outstanding, good or bad, to talk about that this game does any different to any other tradlike. POSITIVES + New Toys Metaprogress - Metaprogress is almost entirely new ships and starting crew types. There is also a mechanic where the more you've filled out of a creature's bestiary, the greater your crit chance against them, but we'll come back to that. It's not a bad mechanic either. + okay. you got me. the space pirate language made me chuckle. NEGATIVES - I'd say Elon Musk permanently ruined the word "grok" but actually anything Robert Heinlein comes up with is probably stinky already. This is the name of the crit mechanic I mentioned earlier and it's closer to Heinlein's meaning than Musk's, where you're critting because you very deeply understand the target. - The fauna hazard rating is meaningless to a new player. - The artstyle... listen. Normally, I don't care about the artstyle of a game too much. But... God, the "Children's Coloring Book from 2005 Special" does not suit the rest of the game. - Don't melee. Seriously. I see you thinking about it. I see you going "but the knife has [i]Path of Achra[/i] attack-on-step! surely passive attacks are good" and I tell you no. Run away if you can. Sniper in one slot, shotgun in the other for closer targets. Melee, ESPECIALLY passive melee, will always betray you. Shame the game starts you with a knife. - Quests that require you to do a thing Only This Module or Weapon Can Do should give you a rental or something. At least let me blow up asteroids with missiles to mine them at a loss a la Rogue Galaxy or something. - The codes that the community discovers for you is cute once. I rapidly learned to hate it after it was tutorialized.
After playing a few hours of this game, my conclusion of this game is, that it is fine! It is safe to play this game.
This is the most boring game I have ever played. I have played every rouge like i can get my hands on. Can't understand the positive reviews.

I don't think it is worth the price. I am a veteran roguelike player, I was looking for something as deep as Taley of May'eyal. Approaching Infinity is very deep and has very promising loop, but all parts of risk-reward equation are severely lacking. Large variety of collectible resources becomes irrelevant, because their individual usability is barely impactful for a run. Large variety of hostile monsters is irrelevant, because as soon as You collect enough gear to be prepared for all their resistances, they are fought all the same. Progression is linear and too simple, it is easy to hoard cash and gear You buy with it grant You static benefit for the rest of the run ( You just have to switch it for specific challenges ).

It's interesting at first glance for the retro feel and expectation of some deep, detailed, story-driven gameplay. Once you get going though it just feels so empty and....hollow I guess is the best way to describe it. Nothing immersing and I just can't lose myself in this for some reason like I can in so many other games like this. There is a lore to the game world but it feels so basic and barebones. 'There was a lost war that was fought here'. OK...care to elaborate? I mean I'm not from here so.... I put a couple hours in and I feel no desire to come back to it. I'm a bit shocked to see the great reviews because I just do not see why. I think the price is way too high for people to really take a chance on this. Refunding.
Just started this game but I can tell it's going to be a gem. Can't wait to surf the stars

It has been a while since I decided to chime in with a Steam review about anything. Yet I am now a few days deep into a gaming binge the likes of which I haven't experienced in years, and Approaching Infinity is the reason for it. Presently the second-smallest game footprint on my hard drive, it still looms large in terms of pure fun. These marathon sessions really take me back to the days when I was making epic pushes to achieve a win at Nethack. Approaching Infinity is not shy about this heritage. Books of lore normally encountered in the early game point the way to a deep deep cave in an advanced sector of space where the Amulet of Yendor purportedly can be found. Yet this game is its own thing far more than a copycat of that epic roguelike. Approaching Infinity puts you in command of a starship, roaming open space and deploying away missions to achieve your goals on various planets and derelict vessels. This artfully makes the most of a modern concept -- the gameplay loop. Some away missions play out a great deal like classic Rogue/Nethack games. Your team consists of multiple crew members, but they all occupy the same space on a map grid. This squad typically sees every member sporting two guns and one melee weapon. Smart use of those weapons along with officer skills, consumables, and even terrain modifiers will make the difference when an away mission encounters hostile combatants delivering truly deadly attacks. Yet after any mission where your captain is not killed, the team regroups aboard ship to handle other matters. Those other matters can involve crafting new gear as well as conducting commerce at various space stations. Progression is a satisfying blend of recruiting more officers/crew, training your officers, and personally gaining levels. All the while you are also swapping out ship systems and away team gear to improve the performance of both. Crafting is downright robust, so if you focus on collecting those materials and skills, a viable endgame strategy is to build your own badass armor, shields, and weapons. Yet Approaching Infinity is also true to the spirit of classic space games in the sense that your destiny is your own. If you really like commerce, set yourself up with loads of cargo capacity, then try to make the most of different bases' prices on trade goods. If you really like piracy, set yourself up with speed and offensive output to prey upon the merchant vessels you encounter. If you prefer to keep space orderly, then become a pirate hunter and bask in the support of well-monied factions. This game will ultimately compel a little of many activities. I did not mention bounty hunting because every seven or so sectors a villainous boss ship guards the lone warp point suitable for departing that sector. These foes can be fought for free, but normally they will be encountered after a chance to accept a big bounty for their elimination. This is a sort of literal gatekeeping so that especially peaceful explorers or traders still must pass a certain threshold of tactical capability before advancing. Of course, Approaching Infinity is big on choice, so if those gate-guarding bosses don't work for you, a modest warp drive upgrade is enough to skip over sectors locked down by unique vessels. As I write all this out, I realize that this game is something of a proper mashup between FTL and Nethack. Victory in Approaching Infinity is normally about achieving a grand personal goal while helping a faction advance their own agenda. Thus even after victory in this challenging roguelike, replay value remains strong. For example, none of the merchant groups will welcome you at their stations if you make a habit of attacking their vessels; but if you instead defend their freighters from piracy, you are sure to become unwelcome at pirate bases. Ultimately, Approaching Infinity is about making your own way in a vast region of space that pairs serious ongoing clashes of alien species, economic cartels, and mystical ideologies with the kind of tongue-in-cheek humor featured in the writing of the best old school roguelikes. It never takes itself too seriously, yet it remains serious enough to become lost in for hour after hour of personalized space opera. Though it offers "Adventure Mode" for players who want to explore the progression and story without the hardcore edge, if you were a fan of those old high stakes roguelikes and you're also a fan of Star Trek/Blake's 7 sorts of serials, then you will almost certainly find it easy to get hooked on the Perma-death mode of Approaching Infinity.
